title: Why Checking Your Investments Too Often Makes You Avoid Them

source.title: MYOPIC LOSS AVERSION AND THE EQUITY PREMIUM PUZZLE
source.authors: Shlomo Benartzi and Richard H. Thaler

intro.summary: This lesson follows one question: why have stocks paid far more than safe bonds over the last century, so much more that standard economics struggles to explain it? Benartzi and Thaler (1993) propose 'myopic loss aversion'. People feel losses about twice as strongly as equal gains, and they check their investments often. Their simulations suggest that checking about once a year makes stocks and bonds feel equally attractive. A large meta-analysis by Brown, Imai, Vieider and Camerer puts the typical loss-aversion number near 1.96, or about 1.74 after a correction for publication bias. A multinational replication by Ruggeri and colleagues found that most of prospect theory's classic choice patterns hold up. The evidence is still disputed. Critics argue that loss aversion may vanish for small stakes, or that it may really be inertia or extra attention to losses, and the 1993 simulations show the explanation is plausible, not that it is proven. Good follow-up topics are probability weighting in prospect theory, the endowment effect, publication bias in meta-analysis, and the 'loss attention' alternative.
background: A stock is a small share of a company whose price can rise or fall a lot. A bond is a loan to a government or company that pays a steadier, smaller return.
A 'risk premium' is the extra average return people demand for holding something whose value swings around.
Standard economics assumes people judge a gamble by averaging how good each possible outcome is, weighted by its chance. This is called expected utility.
Prospect theory, by Kahneman and Tversky, says instead that people judge outcomes as gains or losses from a starting point, and that losses hurt more.
intro.aha: The very same risky investment can feel like a bad deal or a good one depending only on how often you look at it, and checking about once a year is enough to explain why stocks have had to pay several percent more than bonds.

primer.heading: The question: why do stocks pay so much more?
primer.body: Over most of the twentieth century, stocks earned far more each year than very safe government loans. Economists Mehra and Prescott showed that this gap, the 'equity premium', is too big to explain by ordinary fear of risk. People would need to be absurdly afraid of risk to accept it. So the puzzle is why so many people keep holding low-paying bonds at all.
primer.quote: Since 1926, the annual real return on stocks has been about 7 percent while the real return on treasury bills has been less than 1 percent.

primer.heading: The key ingredient: losses loom larger
primer.body: Imagine finding $100, then imagine losing $100. Most people say the loss feels worse than the find feels good. Researchers call this loss aversion. They measure it with one number, λ (lambda), which says how many times heavier a loss weighs than an equal gain. If λ = 2, losing $100 feels about as bad as gaining $200 feels good.
primer.quote: Empirically, losses tend to be treated as if they were twice as large as an equivalent gain.

primer.heading: How big is it, and is it real?
primer.body: One early study of 25 students reported λ = 2.25, and many models simply reused that number. A 2022 meta-analysis combined 607 estimates from 150 papers. It found an average near 1.96, or about 1.74 after correcting for the chance that low results went unpublished. Some researchers doubt loss aversion is general: it may disappear for small amounts, or reflect inertia or extra attention to losses. A replication across 19 countries found that most classic prospect-theory choice patterns still appear, though some are weaker.
primer.quote: The results replicated for 94% of items, with some attenuation.

primer.heading: What Benartzi and Thaler did and found
primer.body: They combined loss aversion with how often people look at their results, which they call the 'evaluation period'. Using real stock, bond and treasury-bill returns from 1926 to 1990, they simulated how good or bad each investment would feel when judged every 1 to 18 months. They then asked how often an investor would have to check for stocks and bonds to feel equally attractive. The answer was about once a year. That is a very ordinary habit, given yearly statements and tax returns.
primer.quote: As the figures show, the horizon at which the prospective utility for stocks is equal to the value for bonds or treasury bills is always between 9 and 12 months, or roughly one year.

primer.heading: Why it matters, and its limits
primer.body: If the idea is right, a large part of the stock premium is the price of looking too often. The authors estimate that someone who judged results only every 20 years would accept a premium of about 1.4% instead of about 6.5%. The work shows the story fits the numbers. It does not prove it: the model uses one person's preferences to stand for whole markets, and the size of λ is still debated.
primer.quote: Of course, there is no way of demonstrating that one particular explanation is correct, so in this paper we perform various tests to determine whether our hypothesis is plausible.

concepts.title: Weighing a bet by its chances
concepts.idea: A gamble's average result is each outcome multiplied by its chance, added up; Samuelson's coin flip (win $200 or lose $100) averages +$50.

predict.question: A stall at a fair offers a game. You have a 1-in-10 chance to win $50. Otherwise you lose $5. On average, what does one play give you?
options: +$45 per play
+$0.50 per play
−$4.50 per play
$0: the big rare prize and the small common loss cancel out
why: This takes the $5 off the $50 without weighting by chance. The prize comes only 1 time in 10, so it adds just 0.1 × $50 = $5 per play.
Right. The win adds 0.1 × $50 = $5 per play and the loss takes 0.9 × $5 = $4.50, so the average is +$0.50. It is slightly in your favour, though any single play gives +$50 or −$5.
This counts only the loss part (0.9 × $5). The rare prize still adds $5 per play, which more than covers it.
It feels balanced, but you have to compute both parts to know. They are $5 against $4.50, so they are not equal and the bet is not fair.

terms.means: The average result per play if you could repeat a bet many times: each outcome times its chance, all added up
A bet that can end in either a gain or a loss, like Samuelson's coin flip

model.title: One bet, split into its pieces
model.note: Teaching model: a bet with only two outcomes, judged in plain dollars, with chances taken at face value. It has no extra feelings about risk or about losses yet. The $200 / $100 coin flip at a 50% chance is Samuelson's bet as Benartzi and Thaler describe it. Every other setting is illustrative, not the papers' data.

steps.say: This picture breaks one coin-flip bet into pieces. The first bar shows what the prize adds once you account for how often you win.
The second bar shows what the possible loss takes away, so it points down.
The last bar adds the two together. It shows what the bet gives you per play, on average.
Three sliders set the bet: the prize, the amount you could lose, and your chance of winning. Watch what a bigger prize does.
The prize bar grew, so the average grew with it.

explore.prompt: Now you set the bets. Change the prize, the loss and the chance, and watch how the two pieces add up to the average.

goals.text: Keep the prize at least twice the size of the loss, but make the bet's average negative
hints: If the prize must stay at least twice the loss, the dollar amounts can't do the job alone. Which other slider is left?
Lower the chance of winning. The win bar shrinks and the loss bar grows at the same time.
The average crosses zero somewhere between a 25% and a 40% chance of winning.

goals.text: Build a fair bet, with an average of zero, in which you win less than half the time and the loss is at least $50
hints: A fair bet has a win part and a loss part of exactly the same size.
If you win less often than you lose, the prize has to be bigger than the loss to balance it.
First pick a chance below 50%. Then raise the prize until the average bar disappears. At a one-in-four chance, the prize must be several times the loss.

feedback.correct: Yes. Weight each outcome by its chance: the rare $50 prize adds $5 per play and the common $5 loss takes $4.50, which leaves +$0.50 on average.
feedback.incorrect: It is tempting to compare the dollar amounts directly, or to judge by gut feeling whether a big rare prize cancels a small common loss. The idea says to multiply each outcome by its chance first and then add: 0.1 × $50 − 0.9 × $5 = +$0.50.

steps.say: Here is Samuelson's bet. Flip a fair coin: heads you win $200, tails you lose $100.
Imagine flipping many times. Half the flips win $200, so the prize adds 0.5 × 200 = $100 per flip on average.
The other half lose $100, so the loss takes away 0.5 × 100 = $50 per flip.
Add the pieces: +100 − 50 = +$50. This sum is called the bet's expected value: each outcome times its chance, added up.
Careful: no single flip ever pays $50. Each flip pays +$200 or −$100. The $50 is the long-run average per flip. A bet that can end in a gain or a loss like this is called a mixed lottery.
Now make the loss bigger. A $300 loss on a fair coin takes away $150 per flip, more than the prize adds. The average falls to −$50.
Chances matter as much as amounts. Back to a $100 loss, but heads now comes up 70% of the time. The win part grows to $140 and the loss part shrinks to $30.
Return to Samuelson's fair coin: +$50 on average, clearly in your favour. Yet his colleague turned it down. Keep that puzzle in mind.

understand.explanation: To weigh a bet, multiply each possible outcome by its chance, then add the results. For Samuelson's coin flip, 0.5 × $200 − 0.5 × $100 = +$50. This is the bet's expected value. It is a long-run average, not what any single play pays: one flip gives either +$200 or −$100. Changing either the amounts or the chances moves the average, and a bet with a big prize can still average a loss if the prize is rare enough. Benartzi and Thaler open their paper with this bet because it has a clearly positive average, yet a thoughtful person refused it. The average by itself does not tell us how people actually feel about a bet.
understand.quote: Consider the problem first posed by Paul Samuelson (1963). Samuelson asked a colleague whether he would be willing to accept the following bet: a 50% chance to win $200 and a 50% chance to lose $100. The colleague turned this bet down, but announced that he was happy to accept 100 such bets.

connect.caption: This is the model's rule, not a formula printed in the papers. Blue p is the chance of winning and green win is the prize; their product is the first bar. Orange loss times the chance of losing, (1 − p), is the second bar. Brown et al. value a two-outcome bet (x, p; y) as w⁺(p)U(x) + w⁻(1−p)U(y). If the weights are just the chances and value is just dollars, that becomes exactly this average. Later concepts change U so losses count more.

concepts.recap: A bet's average is each outcome times its chance, added up: Samuelson's coin flip averages +$50, even though no single flip pays that.

concepts.title: Losses hurt more than gains feel good
concepts.idea: In prospect theory a loss is multiplied by λ, so a bet with a positive average can still feel bad once λ is large enough, as with Samuelson's colleague.

predict.question: A new flip: 50% chance to win $300, 50% chance to lose $100. Someone turns it down. If they judge it with the straight-line rule you just used, what must be true of their λ?
options: λ is above 3
λ is above 2
λ is above 1
Nothing: no one would refuse a bet with a positive average
why: Right: the felt value is ½·300 − ½·λ·100 = 150 − 50λ. That only drops below zero once λ passes 3, when the loss's sting (λ × 100) outweighs the $300 gain.
2 was the tipping point for the $200 win. A bigger $300 win needs a stronger sting to cancel it, so λ = 2 still leaves this flip feeling good (+50).
Any λ above 1 makes losses sting more. But a sting of 1.5 × $100 = 150 is still well under the $300 gain, so the flip would still feel good.
Plain averaging predicts that, since the average here is +$100. Loss aversion is the reason people do refuse such bets: a big enough λ makes the felt value negative.

terms.means: The starting point that outcomes are judged from. Anything above it counts as a gain and anything below it counts as a loss.
The tendency for a loss to feel worse than an equal-sized gain feels good.
The loss aversion coefficient: how many times more a loss counts than an equal gain. λ = 1 means no loss aversion.
The curve that turns each gain or loss into how much it feels worth. It is steeper on the loss side.

model.title: How a coin flip's win and loss feel
model.note: Teaching model: a straight-line ('bi-linear') value curve, the form Benartzi and Thaler use for Samuelson's example. Gains count at face value and losses are multiplied. Full prospect theory also bends the curve (powers of about 0.88) and reweights probabilities; both are left out here. The $200/$100 flip is Samuelson's. The values 2.25 and 2.5 come from the papers. Other numbers are illustrative.

series.label: If losses and gains counted equally

steps.say: Across the bottom is a change in your money. Right means winning, left means losing, and this middle line means no change.
The solid line shows how each change feels. For now, losing feels exactly as bad as winning feels good.
Two dots mark the coin flip from before: win $200 or lose $100.
This slider multiplies how much every loss hurts. Watch the left side tilt down.
The middle dot and its line show how the whole flip feels: half the win plus half the loss. This slider changes the size of the loss.

explore.prompt: You now control two things: how hard losses sting, and how big the loss is. Use them to make the flip feel good, bad or neutral on purpose.

goals.text: Make the loss smaller than $100, yet still make the flip feel like a bad deal (felt value below zero).
hints: A smaller loss is easier to accept, so something else has to make it hurt more.
Watch the 'Felt sting of the loss' box. The flip turns bad once that sting is bigger than the $200 the win feels like.
Pick a loss just under $100, then raise the sting until multiplier × loss passes 200.

goals.text: Make the flip feel almost exactly neutral (felt value within 3 of zero), while losses sting more than twice as much as gains.
hints: Neutral means the half-weighted win and the half-weighted loss cancel out.
That happens when the loss's felt sting (multiplier × loss) equals the felt gain of 200.
Choose a multiplier a little above 2, then shrink the loss until multiplier × loss lands on 200.

feedback.correct: Yes. Refusing means ½·300 < ½·λ·100, so λ × 100 must outweigh the $300 win. That needs λ above 3. The bigger the possible win, the stronger the loss aversion has to be before the bet feels bad.
feedback.incorrect: Work it the same way as the $200 flip. The felt value is ½·300 − ½·λ·100 = 150 − 50λ. The tipping point is not fixed at 2: it is the win divided by the loss. Here that is 300 ÷ 100 = 3, so only someone with λ above 3 would refuse.

steps.say: Start with no extra sting. The $100 loss feels like −100 and the $200 win feels like +200. Half of each gives a felt value of +50, the same as the flip's average.
Everything is judged from this middle line, where your money doesn't change. Prospect theory calls it the reference point. It scores changes as gains or losses, not your total wealth.
Now let losses sting 1.5 times harder. The left side gets steeper and the loss feels like −150. The flip still feels good, at +25.
At twice the sting, the loss feels like −200 and exactly cancels the +200 win. The felt value is 0, yet the average is still +$50.
This extra sting is called loss aversion, and the multiplier is λ (lambda). λ = 1 means a loss counts the same as an equal gain.
Go past 2 and the flip feels bad. At λ = 2.5, the value Benartzi and Thaler used for Samuelson's colleague, it feels like −25. He turned the single bet down.
Tversky and Kahneman's well-known estimate, λ = 2.25, also makes the flip feel bad, at −12.5. The bent line is the value function: straight for gains, kinked at zero, steeper for losses.

understand.explanation: Prospect theory judges each outcome as a gain or a loss from a reference point, and it multiplies losses by λ. For the $200/$100 flip, the felt value is ½·200 − ½·λ·100 = 100 − 50λ. So the flip feels bad once λ passes 2, even though its average stays at +$50. Benartzi and Thaler used exactly this straight-line rule, with λ = 2.5, to show why Samuelson's colleague refused one flip. Tversky and Kahneman's 1992 estimate of 2.25 was a median from just 25 graduate students. Estimates vary between studies and people, and some studies find little loss aversion for small stakes, so 'about 2' is a typical value, not a law. The full theory also bends the curve and reweights chances; this model drops both to show the multiplier on its own.
understand.quote: Empirical estimates of loss aversion are typically in the neighborhood of 2, meaning the disutility of giving something up is twice as great as the utility of acquiring it

equation.text: ·x for losses.   Felt value = ½·200 − ½·

connect.caption: The first part is the 'bi-linear' value function Benartzi and Thaler use (they write U(x) = x for x ≥ 0 and 2.5x for x < 0 in Samuelson's example, and 2.25x in a check). Blue λ is the sting slider and orange L is the size of the loss. The red felt value is the middle dot's height. Full prospect theory uses x^0.88 for gains and −λ(−x)^0.88 for losses, plus probability weights; this model keeps the lines straight.

concepts.recap: Multiply losses by λ: once λ × loss outweighs the gain, a bet with a positive average feels bad, which is why Samuelson's colleague said no.

activities.question: A friend offers a fair coin flip: heads you win $200, tails you lose $100. You get one flip. Would you take it?

options.text: Yes, the average is +$50, so it's a good deal
options.feedback: That is the averaging logic from the last concept. Hold on to it and see how a different way of weighing the flip changes the answer.

options.text: No, losing $100 would feel worse than winning $200 feels good
options.feedback: That is almost word for word what Samuelson's colleague said. Keep it in mind: this lesson puts a number on that feeling.
A fair reaction. The model will show what decides it: how strongly a loss stings compared with a gain.

activities.prompt: Same flip, two people. Compare where the middle dot lands for each.

cases.label: Losses count the same as gains (λ = 1)
Losses count 2.25 times (Tversky and Kahneman's estimate)

activities.takeaway: Back to your first answer. The flip's average is +$50 in both cases. With losses counted 2.25 times, though, it feels like −12.5. If you said no, you reasoned like Samuelson's colleague. Typical estimates put λ near 2, but they vary widely between studies and people.

concepts.title: Combining hundreds of λ estimates
concepts.idea: A meta-analysis pulls each noisy estimate toward the overall average, and pulls harder the larger its standard error, which is why the pooled mean (about 1.96) sits below the raw average and below the famous 2.25.

predict.question: A new study finds λ = 0.6, meaning its people barely mind losses at all. That is far below the average. It tested so many people that its number is sure to within about ±0.1. After it is combined with all the other studies, where does it end up?
options: It stays close to 0.6, nudged up only slightly
It is pulled most of the way up to the average of about 1.8
It stays exactly at 0.6, because only numbers above the average get pulled
It is pushed down, further from the average
why: Right: the pull depends on how unsure a study is. At ±0.1 the pull is under 2%, so the study barely moves (to about 0.62), even though it is far from the average.
Being far from the average is tempting to treat as a reason for a big pull. But a precise study is trusted, so it keeps nearly all of its own number. Distance only matters once the study is unsure.
The walkthrough only showed high numbers coming down, so this is easy to assume. The rule pulls toward the average from either side; the paper notes that values below one are shrunk too.
Combining never pushes a study away from the average. The corrected value always lies between the study's own number and the average.

terms.means: How far a study's estimate would typically wander by luck if the study were run again with new people; smaller samples give bigger standard errors
The share of the way an estimate is moved toward the average of all studies, from 0% (kept as is) to 100% (replaced by the average)
Moving noisy estimates toward the average of all studies, so that results that are extreme only by luck count for less

model.title: One study's λ before and after it is combined with all the others
model.note: Teaching model: it follows one study at a time using the paper's simple pooling rule (equations C.3–C.4, model M1), with the paper's estimated average λ₀ = 1.809 and between-study spread τ = 0.747 held fixed. The real analysis estimates the average, the spread and every study at once, and its preferred model (M2), which groups estimates by paper and allows a skewed spread, gives 1.955. The study on the sliders is made up for illustration; the average (1.809) and 2.25 are the papers' numbers.

steps.say: Each bar is a value of λ, the loss multiplier from the last concept. The first bar is what one study reported.
These two bars stay put. One is the average across hundreds of studies, and the other is the famous 2.25 from a 1992 study of 25 students.
This slider sets the study's own number. Push it up.
This slider says how unsure the study is: how far its number might be off just by luck.
Watch this bar. It shows where the study lands once all the studies are weighed together.

explore.prompt: You have seen how uncertainty decides how far a study gets pulled. Now use it: build a study that starts out extreme and ends up looking ordinary.

goals.text: Take a study that reported more than twice the average λ, and make it end up within 0.3 of the average of all studies after combining.
hints: Which control decides how hard the average pulls on a study?
Keep the study's own number high. Then make the study much less sure of itself and watch the pull percentage climb.
A number that high needs a pull well above three quarters before it gets that close. Keep raising the uncertainty until 'After combining' sits near the average bar.

feedback.correct: Yes. How far a study moves depends first on how unsure it is. A very precise study keeps almost all of its own number, even an unusual one, and the small pull it gets points toward the average from below as well as from above.
feedback.incorrect: Being far from the average does not by itself earn a big pull. The pull is set by the study's uncertainty: at ±0.1 it is under 2%, so a precise 0.6 stays near 0.6. Shrinkage also works in both directions, so a low number is nudged up, never pushed down.

steps.say: Start with a careful study. It reports λ = 3.0 and is sure to within about ±0.1. Combining barely moves it: the pull is about 2%, and it stays near 2.98.
That ± number has a name: the standard error. It says how far the estimate would wander if the study were rerun with new people. Small samples give big standard errors. Raise it to 0.5.
At a standard error of 1, the meta-analysis trusts this study much less. It leans on what all the other studies say, and the study drops to about 2.24.
The pull is called the pooling factor: the share of the way an estimate is moved toward the average. It grows with the standard error. At ±2 it reaches 88%, and the study lands near 1.96.
Moving estimates toward the average like this is called shrinkage. Distance matters too. With the same uncertainty, a study reporting 5 travels much further, about 2.8.

In the real data, the biggest λ values had the biggest standard errors, so they shrank most. That pulled the combined result down to 1.955 in the paper's preferred model, below the raw 1.97 and below 2.25.

understand.explanation: Brown, Imai, Vieider and Camerer gathered 607 estimates of λ from 150 papers. Taken at face value, these estimates average 1.97 and have a median of 1.69. Each estimate also has a standard error, and the meta-analysis uses it to decide how much to trust that estimate. Noisy estimates are pulled toward the average of all studies, and the pull grows with the standard error. Precise ones keep almost their own value. Because the highest estimates were also the least precise, shrinking them lowered the combined mean, to 1.955 in the paper's preferred model (95% credible interval 1.82 to 2.105). That is below the 2.25 many researchers still use, which came from one small 1992 study. The result rests on the model's assumptions, including that the published studies are a fair sample, and the individual studies still differ a lot from one another.
understand.quote: This is meta-analytic pooling at work—estimates that fall far from the mean are shrunk towards more plausible values, with the amount of shrinkage proportional to the standard error.

connect.caption: This is the paper's pooling rule (equations C.3 and C.4). λ_{i} is the study's reported value (first slider) and se_{i} is its standard error (second slider). ω_{i} is the pooling factor, shown as 'Pull toward the average'. λ̂_{i} is the corrected estimate, shown as 'After combining'; the paper writes it with the same letter as the true value. λ_{0} = 1.809 is the average of all studies and τ = 0.747 is how much studies truly differ; both are held fixed here at the paper's model-M1 estimates.

concepts.recap: Combining studies shrinks noisy estimates toward the average; the biggest λ values were the noisiest, so the pooled mean (about 1.96) lands below the raw 1.97 and the famous 2.25.

concepts.title: Is loss aversion real? Support and challenges
concepts.idea: Evidence for loss aversion (meta-analysis, multinational replication, Mrkva et al.) sits alongside serious challenges (small-stakes findings, inertia, loss attention, publication bias), so its size and reach remain contested.

terms.means: Running a study again, with new people, to see whether the original result shows up a second time
When studies with expected or 'exciting' results get published more often than others, so the published record leans one way
A habit of sticking with what you already have or already do, whether or not losing it hurts more than gaining something
The idea that losses make people pay more attention, without making losses count more than equal gains

understand.explanation: Earlier you met λ, the number that says how much more a loss weighs than an equal gain; λ = 1 means no loss aversion. Across 607 published estimates λ is usually above 1, and a large replication (running a study again with new people) of the original prospect-theory questions in 19 countries found the same patterns for most items. Critics answer that with small sums people often show no loss aversion, that psychological inertia (sticking with what you have out of habit) can explain some findings credited to loss aversion, and that losses may simply grab more attention (loss attention) without being weighted more. There is also publication bias, where results that fit expectations get published more readily; one correction for it lowers the average λ from about 1.96 to about 1.74. The fair summary is that loss aversion shows up often, but its size depends on stakes, people and method, and how far it reaches is still argued over. Much of this rests on comparing different studies, so a difference between studies cannot be pinned on one cause.
understand.quote: Multiple studies have questioned the existence of loss aversion. In several studies examining the effect of losses in decision-making, no loss aversion was found under risk and uncertainty.

activities.prompt: Follow the evidence as it built up over 30 years. Each stage adds something, and some stages push back on earlier ones.

stages.label: 1992: the famous 2.25
stages.text: One of the first estimates of λ came from Tversky and Kahneman in 1992. They asked 25 graduate students to make hypothetical (unpaid) choices between bets. The middle value they reported was λ = 2.25, with no average and no measure of spread. Many finance models still plug in 2.25. The meta-analysis authors note it is almost 30 years old and comes from a very small group.

stages.label: 2022: pooling 607 estimates
stages.text: Brown, Imai, Vieider and Camerer collected 607 estimates of λ from 150 articles in economics, psychology, neuroscience and other fields. Their preferred average is 1.955. They report a 95% probability that the true average lies between 1.820 and 2.105. That range leaves out 1 (no loss aversion) and also leaves out 2.25, so the 1992 value looks a bit too high. Of the raw estimates, 93.9% were above 1. The catch is that estimates vary widely, and the study features they recorded (type of experiment, kind of participants, and so on) explain only 15.5% of that spread.

stages.label: 2020: a replication in 19 countries
stages.text: Ruggeri and colleagues repeated the original 1979 prospect-theory questions with 4,098 people in 19 countries and 13 languages. Results replicated for 94% of the questions, though often more weakly than in the original, and 12 of 13 key comparisons held up. Keep in mind that these questions test prospect theory's patterns in general; loss aversion is only one part of that. Separately, Mrkva, Johnson, Gächter and Herrmann found loss aversion in five different samples. They also showed that its size changes in ways theory predicts, which is why their paper says reports of its 'death' are exaggerated.

stages.label: Challenge: small stakes and rival explanations
stages.text: Several studies found no loss aversion when the sums at risk were small. Mukherjee and colleagues call this magnitude-dependent loss aversion. David Gal (2006) argued that the status quo bias and the endowment effect (valuing a thing more once you own it) are better explained by psychological inertia, a habit of staying put, than by losses weighing more. Yechiam and Hochman proposed loss attention instead: losses raise heart rate, widen the pupils and focus the mind, even in small-stakes tasks where people show no loss aversion. Some critics add that loss aversion is the simpler single explanation, so the debate is not settled.

stages.label: Challenge: is the published record tilted?
stages.text: In the meta-analysis, very large λ values tend to come from imprecise studies, and imprecise low values are rare. That lopsided pattern can be a sign of publication bias. A correction for it gives about 1.74 instead of 1.955. Unpublished papers report values about 0.25 lower, roughly 1.73. The authors warn that this lopsided pattern could also appear without any bias, because λ cannot fall below 0. One survey of a representative sample of Americans found a middle λ of 0.99, against 1.84 in a college sample using a similar method. A 2025 re-analysis is titled 'Loss aversion is not robust'; this lesson's sources give only its title, not its details.

activities.takeaway: The evidence keeps finding λ above 1 on average. The live questions are how big it is, for whom, at what stakes, and whether rival explanations account for part of it.

activities.title: Support or challenge?
activities.prompt: Sort each finding. Does it mainly support loss aversion, or mainly challenge its existence, its size or how widely it applies?

groups.label: Challenges its existence, size or reach

cards.text: Pooling 607 estimates gives an average λ of 1.955, with a 95% range of 1.820 to 2.105.
cards.feedback: Supports. The whole range sits above 1, the value for no loss aversion. It does trim the famous 2.25, but trimming the size still leaves losses weighing more than gains.

cards.text: 4,098 people in 19 countries answered the original 1979 questions, and 94% of the items replicated.
cards.feedback: Supports, with a caveat. The original patterns held up across many countries and languages, though often more weakly. These questions test prospect theory as a whole, not only loss aversion.

cards.text: Mrkva and colleagues found loss aversion in five different samples, with its size varying in predictable ways.
cards.feedback: Supports. They found the effect again in new groups, and the way its size changed matched what the theory predicts. That makes the effect look systematic rather than random.

cards.text: In several studies with small amounts of money, no loss aversion appeared.
cards.feedback: Challenges its reach. If the effect disappears at small stakes, then '2 times' is not a universal rule. It may only apply once enough is at risk.

cards.text: Gal argued that people keep what they own mainly out of habit and inertia, not because losing it hurts more.
cards.feedback: Challenges it. This is a rival explanation. If inertia explains the endowment effect and the status quo bias, those findings stop counting as evidence for loss aversion.

cards.text: Losses raise heart rate and pupil size more than equal gains, even in tasks where people show no loss aversion.
cards.feedback: Challenges it. It can look like support, because losses clearly matter more to the body. But this is the loss attention account: losses draw more attention without being weighted more in the choice.

cards.text: Correcting the meta-analysis for possible publication bias lowers the average λ to about 1.74.
cards.feedback: Challenges the size, not the existence. 1.74 is still above 1, so loss aversion remains. But the published average may be inflated, and the authors note the correction itself rests on uncertain assumptions.

cards.text: In a representative survey of Americans, the middle λ was 0.99; in a college sample using a similar method, it was 1.84.
cards.feedback: Challenges its reach. A middle value near 1 means a typical person in that sample showed almost no loss aversion. Results from students may not describe everyone. This is one study, so treat it as a warning sign rather than a verdict.

activities.takeaway: The supports mostly show that λ is above 1 on average. The challenges mostly question how big it is, who shows it, at what stakes, and whether another mechanism is at work.
hints: Ask of each card: does it make losses-weigh-more more believable, or does it offer a reason to doubt it, its size or its reach?
A finding can show that losses matter a lot and still challenge loss aversion, if it says losses matter in a different way, such as through attention.

activities.question: You have seen the support and the challenges. Which summary do you think fits the evidence best?

options.text: Loss aversion is a fixed law of human nature: losses always weigh about 2.25 times as much as gains.
options.feedback: This reading has some support: most estimates are above 1, and the effect has replicated across countries. But the details are wrong. The pooled 95% range (1.820 to 2.105) leaves out 2.25. Estimates vary widely between studies. Several studies find no loss aversion at small stakes, and one representative US sample had a middle λ near 1. 'Always' and 'about 2.25' both go beyond the evidence.

options.text: Loss aversion is real on average, probably around 1.7 to 2, but its size depends on the stakes, the people and the method.
options.feedback: This reading fits the meta-analysis, the bias-corrected values (about 1.73 to 1.74), and Mrkva and colleagues' finding that the size varies predictably. Its limits: the pooled data are mostly published studies, the bias correction rests on uncertain assumptions, and a 2025 re-analysis argues the effect is not robust. Rival accounts such as loss attention and inertia could also explain part of what gets counted as loss aversion.

options.text: Loss aversion is mostly an illusion: inertia and attention to losses explain the findings.
options.feedback: This reading draws on real work: Gal's inertia argument, the loss attention research, the small-stakes null results and the 2025 re-analysis. Its limits: in the meta-analysis, 93.9% of the 607 raw estimates were above 1, and many come from bets that mix gains and losses, where λ is measured directly. Mrkva and colleagues also replicated loss aversion in five samples. Some researchers also argue loss aversion is the simpler explanation. 'Mostly an illusion' would need these results explained away too.

options.text: The evidence conflicts so much that we cannot say anything about loss aversion.
options.feedback: This reading takes the disagreement seriously, which is fair. But it throws away information. Hundreds of studies narrow the plausible average a lot. The debate is mainly about size, reach and mechanism, not about whether anything at all is going on. Uncertainty about the details is not the same as knowing nothing.

concepts.recap: Loss aversion shows up in most studies, with λ around 1.7 to 2 on average, but small-stakes results, rival explanations and possible publication bias keep its size and reach in dispute.

concepts.title: One bet feels bad, two together feel good
concepts.idea: With loss aversion, looking at several bets as one combined result makes losses rarer and smaller relative to gains, so someone who refuses one coin flip can rationally welcome two or more taken together.

predict.question: Samuelson's colleague (losses count 2.5 times as much as gains) agrees to take four flips as one bundle. Then he changes his mind about how to follow it: he will hear each result as it lands and feel each flip on its own. How does the deal feel to him now?
options: Bad again: each flip judged alone is the same single bet he refused
Still good, because the money he ends up with is exactly the same
Even better, because watching gives him four chances to enjoy a win
It depends on whether the first flip comes up heads
why: Right. Judged one at a time, each flip feels like −$25 at a loss weight of 2.5, so four separate flips feel like about −$100. The bundle only felt good because its outcomes were combined before they were felt.
The money is the same, which is why this is tempting. But the felt value depends on how outcomes are grouped before they are judged, and felt one by one, each loss gets its full 2.5 weight.
More chances to enjoy a win also means more chances to feel a loss. With losses weighted 2.5 times, each separate flip feels worse than it feels good.
Feeling each flip on its own makes every flip the refused single bet, whatever the order. The first result does not change how the other three are felt.

terms.means: How a person groups outcomes before judging them: one flip at a time, or several flips as one combined total
The informal ways people label, group and judge money results such as bets, purchases and investments

model.title: A bundle of coin flips: the good side against the bad side
model.note: Teaching model: each flip is the paper's bet (50% chance to win $200, 50% chance to lose $100). Gains count at face value and losses are multiplied by the loss weight. This is the simple two-part rule Benartzi and Thaler use for this example (they use a weight of 2.5). It leaves out the curved value function and the probability weighting of full prospect theory. The bundle is judged only as one combined total. Dollar amounts follow exactly from the bet. The loss weights on the slider are illustrative, not measured values.

controls.label: Loss weight: how many times a lost dollar counts

outputs.label: Bad side: losses at face value
Loss weight that makes this bundle a toss-up

bars.label: Bad side: losses at face value
Bad side: losses as they feel

steps.say: Every flip here is Samuelson's bet: heads you win $200, tails you lose $100. These bars weigh up a bundle of such flips.
The first bar is the good side: the gains, averaged over every way the flips can land. The middle bar does the same for the losses.
The last bar shows how those losses feel. This slider sets how many times a lost dollar counts compared with a won one.
This slider adds flips to the bundle. Watch all three bars move.
This box gives the bundle's felt value: the good side minus how the bad side feels.

explore.prompt: Make the loss weight as harsh as the slider allows, then try bundles of different sizes. How many flips does it take before the bundle feels worth it?

goals.text: At the strongest loss weight the slider allows, find the smallest bundle that still feels worth taking (felt value above zero).
hints: Which slider sets how strongly losses count? Push it all the way up first.
At that weight, add flips one at a time and watch whether the felt value box turns positive.
Compare the toss-up loss weight box with your loss weight: you want the first bundle whose toss-up weight is higher than yours.

feedback.correct: Yes. The bundle felt good only because its outcomes were added up before they were felt. Feel each flip on its own and every one is the refused single bet again, at about −$25 each.
feedback.incorrect: You may have reasoned that the same money must feel the same. With loss aversion it does not: the felt value depends on how outcomes are grouped. Judged one flip at a time, every loss gets its full 2.5 weight, and each flip feels bad.

steps.say: Start with one flip and a loss weight of 1, so a lost dollar counts the same as a won one. Gains average $100 and losses average $50, so the felt value is +$50. That is the plain average from earlier.
Now give losses the weight the paper uses for Samuelson's colleague, 2.5. The $50 of losses now feels like $125, more than the $100 good side. Felt value: −$25. He turns the bet down.
Bundle two flips and judge them as one total. Three results are possible: +$400 (one chance in four), +$100 (two in four) and −$200 (one in four). The chance of ending behind falls from 50% to 25%.
The good side has grown to $150, but the felt bad side is still $125. The felt value turns positive at +$25. Same person, same loss weight: now he says yes.

Grouping outcomes before judging them is an aggregation rule. It is one part of mental accounting, the informal ways people code and judge money results. When losses weigh more, the rule you use changes the answer.
Six flips: $337.50 of gains against only $37.50 of losses at face value, and losing results happen about 11% of the time. Even felt at 2.5 times, the bad side is small.
Look at the toss-up box: someone would need a loss weight of 9 to refuse this bundle. Every flip has the same odds as before. Only the grouping changed.

understand.explanation: Samuelson's colleague refused one flip (win $200 or lose $100) but said he would gladly take 100 of them. If a lost dollar counts 2.5 times as much as a won one, his answer hangs together. One flip feels like −$25. Two flips judged as one total feel like +$25, because the only losing result now has a one-in-four chance and the gains have grown. The odds of each flip never change; what changes is how the outcomes are grouped before they are felt. Benartzi and Thaler argue that with loss aversion such grouping rules are not neutral, and they show it with this worked example and its $400 / $100 / −$200 bundle. Two caveats. Samuelson proved this pattern is inconsistent with expected utility theory, so it is sensible only given these loss-averse preferences. And the 2.5 weight is the paper's illustration, not a measurement.
understand.quote: Because of the presence of loss aversion, these aggregation rules are not neutral. This point can best be illustrated by example.

check.task: Put the model in a state where the bundle feels worth taking to someone at least as loss averse as Samuelson's colleague, even though they would end up behind more often than one time in four.
check.hint: Step through the bundle sizes one at a time and watch the chance of ending behind. It does not fall at every step.
check.misconception: Bundling works only by making losses rarer. In fact it works because gains grow large next to the felt losses. With four flips, losing results become more common again (about 31%), yet the bundle still feels good.

connect.caption: The paper writes the colleague's utility as U(x) = x for gains and 2.5x for losses. Here the 2.5 is the loss weight slider λ. Each outcome x_k has k wins among n flips and comes with its chance p_k. V, the felt value box, adds up U(x_k) × p_k over all outcomes of the bundle.

concepts.recap: With loss aversion, judging bets together rather than one at a time can turn a refused gamble into a welcome one.

concepts.title: Check less often, and stocks look better
concepts.idea: Stretching the evaluation period bundles more months of returns, so losses appear less often; with λ around 2, stocks and bonds feel equal at an evaluation period of roughly one year, which accounts for the large equity premium.

predict.question: A pension fund will exist for decades. Its manager must report results every quarter, and like most people feels losses about twice as strongly as gains. Compared with what the fund's long life would justify, how will the manager tend to invest?
options: More in bonds than the fund's long life justifies
More in stocks, because the fund lasts for decades
No difference: how often you report doesn't change the returns
All in stocks, because quarterly reports show more gains
why: Right: the manager feels each quarterly result, and over three months stocks often show a loss that hurts about twice as much, so bonds feel safer. The paper calls this an agency problem that creates myopic loss aversion.
The fund's life is long, but the manager is judged quarter by quarter. What matters for feelings is the evaluation period, not the planning horizon.
The returns are indeed the same, but how they feel is not. Bundling fewer months into each look makes losses show up more often, and each one stings more than a gain pleases.
Short looks show losses more often, not less. Over one quarter a stock dips quite often, which is exactly what makes it feel worse than a bond.

terms.means: How much time passes between the moments you look at an investment and feel its gain or loss. It is not the same as how long you plan to hold it.
Loss aversion combined with looking at results often. It makes risky investments feel worse than they really are over the long run.
The extra return that stocks have paid over safer bonds or treasury bills. In US data since 1926 it was about 6.5% a year above 5-year bonds.

model.title: How good a stock and a bond feel, by months between looks
model.note: Teaching model: returns over a stretch of months are bell-shaped (normal), built from illustrative monthly averages and swings (stock 0.9% ± 6%, bond 0.4% ± 1.5%). Each look is scored with a straight-line value: gains count once and losses count λ times, using true probabilities. The paper also tested this simplified version. Its main results instead used real 1926–1990 US returns, a curved value function and probability weights. The monthly numbers were chosen so the crossings land near the paper's reported simple-version results (about 8 months at λ = 2.25, and λ ≈ 2.77 for a 12-month crossing). The curve heights are illustrative, not the paper's data.

controls.label: How much more a loss hurts (λ)

outputs.label: Chance a look at the stock shows a loss

y.label: How good it feels (gains minus λ-weighted losses, %)

steps.say: This curve shows how good a stock feels to someone who dislikes losses. The further right you go, the more months pass between looks at it.
This one is a bond. Its returns are smaller and steadier.
This slider sets how many months pass between looks. The dots show how each investment feels at that spacing.
This is λ from before: how many times more a loss hurts than an equal gain pleases.
This box gives the chance that a look at the stock shows a loss.

explore.prompt: Play with how often the investor looks, and with how much losses hurt. Watch where the stock and the bond swap places.

goals.text: Keep λ at the classic 2.25 and find how often someone must look for the stock and the bond to feel about the same.
hints: Leave λ alone. Which other slider changes how a stock feels?
Watch the 'Stock minus bond' box: it is negative when you look often and positive when you look rarely.
The box changes sign somewhere between half a year and a full year.

goals.text: For an investor who looks once a year, find how strongly losses must hurt for the stock and the bond to feel about the same.
hints: Set the looks to once a year. Which other slider can tilt the balance back toward the bond?
Raising λ makes every loss sting more, and the stock has more losses to sting.
The balance point lies a little above the classic 2.25 but below 3.

feedback.correct: Yes. The manager feels each quarterly result. Over a quarter, stocks show losses often, and loss aversion makes each one sting about twice as much. So bonds feel better even though the fund could easily wait out the dips.
feedback.incorrect: It is tempting to think only the long-run returns matter. But feelings come from each look, and a quarterly look bundles only three months. Losses show up often at that spacing, so the stock feels worse than the fund's long life would justify.

steps.say: Start with λ = 1, so losses count exactly like gains. The stock's higher average wins at every spacing, and its curve sits above the bond's everywhere.
Now make losses hurt 2.25 times as much, and look every month. A month of stock returns is a loss about 44% of the time, and each loss stings hard. The stock now feels worse than the bond.
Look every 6 months instead. Each look now bundles six months, so good and bad months cancel out and losses show up less often. The time between looks is called the evaluation period.
At 8 months the curves cross, and the stock and the bond feel the same. The paper's simple straight-line version, with λ = 2.25, also lands at 8 months.
At 12 months the stock clearly feels better. Nothing about the stock changed: same returns, same λ. Only how often it is looked at changed.
Go back to monthly looks and the very same stock feels bad again. Disliking losses plus looking often is called myopic loss aversion.
With yearly looks and λ near 2.7 (the paper: 2.77), the two balance at one year. So yearly lookers demand that stocks pay extra: the equity premium, about 6.5% a year.

understand.explanation: Each look at an investment adds up all the months since the last look into one result. Over one month a stock often shows a loss, and each loss is felt about twice as strongly, so it feels worse than a steady bond. Over a year the good months usually outweigh the bad ones, so the stock shows a loss less often and feels better. Benartzi and Thaler ran simulations on real US returns from 1926–1990, using Tversky and Kahneman's prospect theory parameters (λ = 2.25). They found that stocks and bonds feel equal when portfolios are evaluated every 9 to 12 months, roughly once a year (8 months in their simplest straight-line version). That fits the roughly 6.5% a year extra that stocks paid, whereas standard risk aversion would need implausibly extreme values. This shows the explanation is plausible, not proven. The authors say no single explanation can be shown to be correct, and later work still debates how large λ really is.
understand.quote: Using simulations we find that the size of the equity premium is consistent with the previously estimated parameters of prospect theory if investors evaluate their portfolios annually.

check.task: Without touching the loss slider, make the stock feel better than the bond by more than 1 point.
check.hint: Losses hurt just as much as before. What else changes how often a loss turns up when you look?
check.misconception: That the only way to make stocks attractive is to feel losses less, and that how often you look can't matter because the investment itself is unchanged.

connect.caption: x_{i} is a possible return over one look of n months (the months slider), and p_{i} is its chance. Gains count once and losses count λ times (the λ slider). This is the bi-linear form with true probabilities that the paper tested in Section 4. Its main value function, equation (1), instead raises gains and losses to the power 0.88, uses λ = 2.25 and swaps p_{i} for decision weights π_{i}. The gap box compares V for the stock and for the bond.

concepts.recap: The same stock feels bad if you look monthly and worth it if you look yearly. Loss-averse investors who look about once a year explain why stocks have paid several percent more than bonds.

activities.prompt: Two investors own the very same stock and feel losses equally (λ = 2.25). One looks every month and one looks once a year. Compare how the stock feels to each.
activities.takeaway: Same returns, same feelings about loss. The monthly looker sees a loss far more often and finds the stock worse than the bond; the yearly looker finds it better.
